After a long day wrangling pacenotes and wrestling my way through gravel hairpins, I like to cool down with something slower — but still surprisingly strategic. Some nights, I’ll sit cross-legged on the floor of my Auckland apartment, a board spread out in front of me, small carved pieces lined up like miniature rally cars ready for the start line. My hands move the pieces almost instinctively, reading the 'track' ahead like I would in a rally stage, anticipating traps and plotting overtakes. It’s not about high-octane speed here, but about reading my opponent, setting up moves three turns ahead. When I finally clinch a win, there’s a quiet thrill that almost feels like nailing a perfect split time — only this time, the audience is just me and the person across the board. Funny how strategy follows you everywhere, even when the roar of the engine is replaced by the soft clack of wood on wood.

Lately I've been packing my schedule so tight between training, car setup checks, press events, and actual rally stages that I’ve barely had time to breathe. Even when we land in a new country for a leg, I used to sneak in a day to explore the local scene, maybe hunt down a spot that’s been on my wish list for ages—you know, those rare places doing crazy creative cross-country flavors that win all the top awards. Now it feels like I just race, crash at the hotel, repeat. I’m worried I’m burning out before the season’s even halfway.
